lines.text: A law firm is a professional partnership where solicitors and barristers practise law. In the English legal system, solicitors handle most direct client contact — providing legal advice, drafting documents, negotiating contracts, and managing property transactions (conveyancing). Barristers are specialists in courtroom advocacy, typically instructed by solicitors to represent clients in court. This split profession is unique to England and Wales — most other countries have a single legal profession. Law firms range from small high-street practices handling everyday matters (wills, divorces, property sales) to international 'Magic Circle' firms (Clifford Chance, Linklaters) managing billion-pound corporate deals. Inside a firm, the hierarchy runs from trainee solicitors through associates and senior associates to partners, who share the firm's profits. Support staff include paralegals (who assist with legal research and document preparation), legal secretaries, and clerks. Key activities include drafting contracts, conducting due diligence (thorough investigation before a deal), litigation (taking legal disputes to court), mediation (resolving disputes without court), and compliance (ensuring businesses follow regulations). Legal fees are charged by the hour, as fixed fees, or on a conditional basis ('no win, no fee'). Understanding legal vocabulary is valuable not just for lawyers — it helps anyone navigating contracts, property purchases, employment disputes, or business regulations in English-speaking countries.

lines.text: The split profession is uniquely English. Solicitors advise and prepare; barristers advocate in court. Barristers wear wigs and gowns in higher courts — a centuries-old tradition. Since 2004, solicitors can also appear in higher courts with additional qualifications ('solicitor-advocates').

lines.text: Legal aid — government-funded legal assistance for those who can't afford lawyers — has been significantly cut in England and Wales since 2013. Understanding 'legal aid eligibility', 'means testing', and 'access to justice' is important for following social policy debates.

lines.text: 'No win, no fee' (conditional fee agreements) allows clients to pursue claims without upfront costs — the lawyer takes a percentage only if the case wins. Originally for personal injury claims, it's now used in employment and consumer disputes.
